A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original polynomial-learning experiments, BERT and UL2 training and downstream evaluations, ablations, and stability simulations.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds stacking-operator comparisons, attention-head and MLP subnetwork experiments, and BERT throughput measurements.

M1.justification: v1 implements depth-based Random Path Training while mentioning other subnetwork axes as possibilities. v2 Section 4.3 introduces concrete Attention-RaPTr and MLP-RaPTr procedures: progressively selecting random attention heads or subsets of four MLP partitions. These substantially extend the implemented method beyond depth; the original depth procedure and scaling mechanism remain.

E1.justification: The polynomial setting, BERT training corpora and GLUE tasks, UL2 training mixture, and downstream QA/completion/SuperGLUE coverage remain. The new method variants and timing measurements do not introduce new datasets or task requirements.

E2.justification: Beyond v1's standard training, gradual stacking, and PLD comparisons, v2 Table 2 evaluates depth-growth versions of bert2BERT, MSG, LEMON, and MSG with layer interpolation. Table 5 additionally compares against MSG's attention-head and MLP growth operators, substantially expanding the evaluated comparator set.

E3.justification: v2 adds 300k-step BERT comparisons, including 6-9-12 attention-head and 768-1536-3072 MLP schedules, and specifies a common learning-rate schedule for the stacking variants. The reported BERT-Large peak-learning-rate grid narrows from {1, 1.6, 2.5} times 10^-4 to {1, 1.6} times 10^-4; this does not establish that retained experiments were rerun. Most existing protocols remain.

E4.justification: v2 adds BERT throughput analysis but removes the UL2 unmodified-learning-rate ablation and the no-warmup columns from the extensive downstream table. The four-task warmup comparison remains in Table 6. Existing schedule, fixed-layer, scaling, polynomial, and stability analyses are largely retained or relocated.

E5.justification: Both versions report averages across three runs for representative UL2 settings and parenthesized variability. The new BERT tables extend the existing variability-reporting style, without documenting a new statistical procedure, increased run count, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Substantial new results appear in v2 Tables 2, 5, and 11. At 300k steps with the 6-9-12 depth schedule, RaPTr and LEMON both report 1.83 loss, with downstream averages of 84.6 and 84.7. The attention-head comparison reports 1.84 loss for Attention-RaPTr versus 2.07 for MSG. BERT throughput results are added, while UL2 equal-FLOP baseline rows and several ablation entries are removed. Most matched earlier scores remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Lemma 5.4 gains finite-input-set, dimension, and high-probability conditions, and some asserted loss lower bounds become statements that such gaps can occur. Appendix H replaces the earlier single-layer norm lemma with multilayer concentration results and supporting proofs. Appendix G adds an implementation-overhead derivation. The central stability bound and the polynomial and scaling theory otherwise remain substantially unchanged.

C1.justification: v2 broadens its stated contributions to Random Part Training across model axes and a distributed implementation, and explicitly claims the first theoretical framework for stagewise layer dropping. It also narrows the abstract's UL2 improvement from 1-5% to 1.5% and changes the overall conclusion from superiority over stacking to competitiveness with stacking.

C2.justification: v2 interprets observed loss decreases relative to prior loss-preserving growth approaches and adds that stacking may share the polynomial setting's simple-to-complex bias. It more explicitly identifies unresolved schedule selection and the lack of a theoretical explanation for UL2's initial full-model warmup. Earlier limitations concerning loss decreases and inductive bias remain.

D1.justification: New Appendix G details distributed-training difficulties and a shared-subnetwork implementation using linear combinations of layer parameters. v2 also discloses BERT TPU configuration, UL2 sequence length and token budget, the UL2 learning-rate search, and implementation details for additional comparators. These substantially expand reproducibility information, although explicit polynomial stage lengths supplied in v1 are omitted.

R1.justification: v2 substantially develops positioning around dropping versus stacking, explains relationships to bert2BERT, MSG, and LEMON, and connects its stability analysis to loss-preserving growth and dropout/generalization theory. It adds an explicit theoretical-priority claim and discussion of nested-network work. These changes exceed citation or bibliographic updates.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten, Sections 3 and 5 are reframed, and the experimental narrative is reorganized. The former takeaways section is redistributed, related work and broader impact move partly into appendices, and the umbrella terminology changes from Random Path Training to Random Part Training.

P2.justification: The main text and references change from two-column to single-column layout. v2 adds comparison and throughput tables and a distributed-implementation diagram, restructures the UL2 tables, and combines an annotated existing training curve with the stability plots in Figure 3. Several retained figures and tables move into appendices.

improvement.justification: The additional growth-operator comparisons and tested attention/MLP variants substantially strengthen claims that v1 supported mainly through depth experiments against gradual stacking and PLD. Appendix G's concrete implementation and the added BERT timing evidence also improve practical reproducibility. Useful UL2 controls and ablation entries are lost, but the broader validation and more appropriately qualified stacking conclusion provide a substantial net improvement.
